name: Grade 9
theme: Revelation and Scripture; Who is Jesus Christ?

lessons.title: The desire for God
lessons.idea: Human beings are religious by nature. Our longing for truth, goodness, beauty and love points beyond this world, and reason can reach God as its source. Augustine: “our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
lessons.question: What experiences in your life raise the question of God?
lessons.activity: “Wonder journal” (30 min). Students write a one-page reflection on a moment of wonder, longing or gratitude (a sunset, music, friendship). They underline the part that felt bigger than the moment. In small groups they share one sentence and look for common themes. Read Acts 17:22–28.
teach: “The desire for God is written in the human heart” (CCC 27). Humans are “capable of God” and made for communion with him (CCC 27–30). Man is a religious being.
Paul in Athens (Acts 17) begins with the Athenians’ own search: “In him we live and move and have our being.” Wisdom 13:1–9 says that from the beauty of creation we can know its author.
Reason can know God from the world and from the human person: the order of the world, conscience, the desire for happiness (CCC 31–36). It remains limited and clouded by sin (CCC 37–38).
Avoid presenting this as proof that forces belief; it is an invitation to consider.
talk: What experiences point beyond the world?
What does it mean that faith is both gift and free act?
What objection do you hear most?
quiz: Which claim does the Church make about reason and God?|Reason alone shows the Trinity|Reason is useless|Only the baptized can reason|Reason can know that God exists as the source of all, while revelation tells us who he is (CCC 36, 50)|3|CCC 36, 50–53.
The “desire for God” (CCC 27) is best described as…|Written in the human heart because we are made by and for God|Cultural only|A trick|A passing mood|0|CCC 27–30.
Paul’s speech in Acts 17 begins by…|Quoting Moses|Noting the Athenians’ search for God and quoting their poets|Condemning idols|Reading Scripture|1|Acts 17:22–28.
lessons.life: Write a one-page reflection: “What would I need to see for faith to make sense?”
lessons.saint: Edith Stein: philosopher who found faith through reason and suffering.
misc: “Religion is just a crutch invented by weak people.”
“If reason can reach God, we don’t need revelation.”
lessons.mem: “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” (St Augustine, Confessions 1.1)
lessons.hook: Ask students to write privately the thing they most want in life. Then ask: “Once you have it, what do you want next?” Notice the pattern of unending desire.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain in a paragraph how human desire points to God.

lessons.title: Ways to know God by reason
lessons.idea: From creation and the human person, reason can know that God exists. Thomas Aquinas’ five ways argue from motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection and order. They are arguments of reason, which faith builds on and completes.
lessons.question: What are the limits of proof for God?
lessons.activity: “Test the arguments” (35 min). In groups, read short summaries of two of Aquinas’ ways (motion and contingency). Each group states the argument in plain steps, finds one strength and one objection, and presents. Class discusses what the argument shows (a first cause) and what it doesn’t (the Trinity).
teach: The Church teaches that God can be known with certainty by natural reason (Vatican I; CCC 36). Romans 1:19–20: “his invisible nature… has been clearly perceived in the things that have been made.”

Aquinas’ five ways (Summa I, q. 2, a. 3) are about the existence of God as first mover, first cause, necessary being, source of perfection and ordering intelligence (CCC 34). They don’t describe God’s inner life.
Other paths: the cosmos, the moral law and conscience, beauty (CCC 31–34). These are “proofs” in the sense of converging reasons.
Be honest about limits: arguments do not replace faith and may fail to persuade everyone. Faith knows more than reason can reach (CCC 50).
talk: What does reasoning to God not yet tell us?
quiz: Aquinas’ “five ways” argue to God from…|Features of the world such as motion, causation, contingency, degrees and order|Scripture|Feelings|Miracles|0|CCC 34.
What do the five ways NOT prove?|That God is the first cause|That the world depends on another|That reason can reach God|The Trinity or the Incarnation, which need revelation|3|CCC 50.

Which objection do these arguments most directly face?|“An infinite chain of causes needs no first cause”|Science exists|The world has no cause|God is love|0|The reply distinguishes essentially ordered causes.
lessons.life: Summarize one argument in 100 words and test it on a friend.
lessons.saint: Thomas Aquinas: the Dominican friar who wrote the Summa Theologiae and hymns for the Eucharist.
misc: “Arguments for God are all just guesses.”
lessons.mem: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims his handiwork.” (Psalm 19:1)
lessons.hook: Show a line of dominoes. “What knocked over the first one? Can the chain go back forever?” Introduce the idea of a first cause.
lessons.assess: Ask students to summarize one of the five ways and note one strength and one limit.

lessons.title: Faith is reasonable and free
lessons.idea: Faith is a personal adherence to God and assent to all he has revealed. It is a gift of grace, a free act of the human person, and consistent with reason. Doubt is not the opposite of faith but can lead to deeper faith.
lessons.question: Does faith require certainty? Do doubts mean unbelief?
lessons.activity: “Doubt conversation” (35 min). A structured conversation. Read John 20:24–29 and Mark 9:24. Questions: What did Thomas need? What did Jesus give? What is the difference between doubt and unbelief? What helps when I doubt? Students write one honest question for God, and one step to seek an answer.
teach: Faith is “a personal adherence of man to God… and a free assent to the whole truth that God has revealed” (CCC 150). It is a supernatural gift that precedes our decision (CCC 153–155).
Faith is reasonable: there are signs of credibility (miracles, prophecies, the Church’s holiness) (CCC 156). Faith and science do not conflict (CCC 159).
It is also free: no one can be forced to believe (CCC 160, 2106). Doubt can be voluntary (a refusal) or involuntary (a difficulty); the second is not a sin (CCC 2088).
Hebrews 11 lists the faithful. Faith grows through prayer, sacraments and community (CCC 162).
talk: What is the difference between doubt and unbelief?
What do you do with unanswered questions?
quiz: Faith in the Catechism is…|Blind trust|A feeling|A personal adherence to God and assent to all he has revealed, a gift of grace and a free act (CCC 150, 153–155)|Opinion|2|CCC 150, 153–155.

The father in Mark 9:24 prays “I believe; help my unbelief.” What does this show?|Faith can coexist with difficulty and still ask for grace|Faith excludes doubt|Doubt is sin|He had no faith|0|Mark 9:24; CCC 2088.
Voluntary doubt differs from involuntary doubt in that the former…|Is a deliberate refusal to hold what is revealed (CCC 2088)|Is rare|Is harmless|Is a difficulty|0|CCC 2088.
lessons.life: List three questions you have about faith and take one to a trusted catechist or priest.
lessons.saint: Thérèse of Lisieux: faith through darkness.
misc: “Having doubts means I’ve lost my faith.”
lessons.mem: “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is trusting a friend reasonable? Is it free?” Both. Faith in God is like trust, but supernaturally given.
lessons.assess: Ask students to define faith and distinguish doubt from unbelief.

lessons.title: Revelation in history
lessons.idea: God reveals himself in history, in deeds and words that explain each other, step by step. He speaks through creation, to Adam and Noah, Abraham, Moses and the prophets, and finally in his Son Jesus Christ, who is the fullness of revelation.
lessons.question: Why a gradual revelation?
lessons.activity: “Build a timeline” (30 min). Students build a timeline of revelation: creation, Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, prophets, Jesus, apostles. For each, add the event, God’s self-disclosure (e.g., his name at the burning bush) and the Scripture reference. Read Hebrews 1:1–2.
teach: Revelation is God’s self-communication (CCC 50–53). He does it by deeds and words intimately connected (CCC 53, 2). It unfolds in stages (CCC 54–64).
Christ is the fullness: “No one has ever seen God; the only Son… has made him known” (John 1:18; CCC 65–66). There will be no new public revelation after the apostles (CCC 66).
“Private revelations” (e.g., Fatima, Lourdes) do not add to the deposit of faith; they help us live it (CCC 67).
The response to revelation is the obedience of faith (CCC 142–143).
talk: What is public vs private revelation?
quiz: The “fullness” of revelation is…|The Bible alone|The Church fathers|Moses|Jesus Christ (Hebrews 1:1–2; CCC 65)|3|CCC 65–66.
God reveals himself through…|Deeds and words intimately connected (CCC 53)|Philosophers|Dreams|Words only|0|CCC 53.
Private revelations such as Fatima or Lourdes…|Add to the deposit of faith|Are required belief|Contradict Scripture|Do not add to revelation but may help us live it (CCC 67)|3|CCC 67.
lessons.life: Read Hebrews 1:1–4 and write a summary.
lessons.saint: John of the Cross: a Carmelite poet and mystic who wrote about God’s presence in darkness.
misc: “God revealed himself only through the Bible.”
lessons.mem: “In many and various ways God spoke of old to our fathers by the prophets; but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son.” (Hebrews 1:1–2)
lessons.hook: Show a photo album arranged chronologically. “What do you learn about a person by seeing how they act over time?” God teaches us himself through history.
lessons.assess: Ask students to place five stages of revelation in order and explain how Christ is the fullness.

lessons.title: Sacred Tradition and Scripture
lessons.idea: Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition flow from the same divine source and together form one sacred deposit of the Word of God. Tradition is the living transmission of the Gospel in the Church, not a list of old customs.
lessons.question: How are Scripture and Tradition related?
lessons.activity: “Two streams” (30 min). Students analyze 2 Thessalonians 2:15, 2 Timothy 2:2 and John 21:25 to find the role of spoken and written teaching. Write a one-page summary: What is Tradition? What is Scripture? How do they relate?
teach: “Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture are bound closely together… they flow out of the same divine wellspring” (CCC 80–82; Dei Verbum 9). Together they form the deposit of faith (CCC 84).
The apostles handed on what they received orally and in writing (CCC 75–79). Not everything Jesus said and did was written (John 21:25), and the Church’s living Tradition preserves the whole.
Tradition includes doctrine, liturgy, the Creed, Church Fathers and the Magisterium (CCC 78). It must be distinguished from ecclesiastical traditions, which can change (CCC 83).
Show the difference from sola scriptura: the canon itself was decided by the Church’s Tradition.
talk: What would be lost without Tradition?
What would be lost without Scripture?
quiz: “Sacred Tradition” in Catholic teaching is…|A second Bible|Local habit|Old customs|The living handing on of the Gospel by the apostles and their successors (CCC 78)|3|CCC 75–79.
Which would NOT be part of the deposit of faith?|A diocesan fasting rule (a changeable discipline)|The Creed|The Real Presence|The Trinity|0|CCC 83.
2 Thessalonians 2:15 matters in this lesson because it…|Forbids writing|Rejects tradition|Defines infallibility|Commends both spoken and written apostolic teaching|3|2 Thessalonians 2:15.
lessons.life: Find three Christian practices not explicit in Scripture (e.g., the canon, Sunday).
lessons.saint: Vincent of Lérins: a monk who taught that the faith is what has been believed “everywhere, always, by all.”
misc: “Tradition is man-made customs that contradict the Bible.”
lessons.mem: “Stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by letter.” (2 Thessalonians 2:15)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How do you know what your great-grandparents were like?” Written letters and stories told within a family. Both are needed.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how Scripture and Tradition relate and give an example.

lessons.title: The Magisterium
lessons.idea: The Magisterium is the Church’s teaching office, the Pope and the bishops in union with him, who authentically interpret the Word of God. It is a servant of the Word, not above it. Teaching comes with different levels of authority and calls for different levels of assent.
lessons.question: What does infallibility mean (and not mean)?
lessons.activity: “Levels of assent chart” (35 min). Students build a chart: (1) dogmas defined as divinely revealed, requiring the assent of faith; (2) definitive doctrines requiring firm acceptance; (3) authoritative non-definitive teaching requiring religious submission of mind and will; (4) prudential decisions. Give examples at each. Read Matthew 16:18–19 and John 21:15–17.
teach: The Magisterium interprets the Word of God authentically (CCC 85–87). Its authority is exercised by the Pope and bishops (CCC 888–892).

Infallibility: when the Pope speaks ex cathedra, or the bishops in an ecumenical council define a doctrine of faith or morals, they are preserved from error (CCC 891). The Pope is not infallible in everything.
The faithful give “the obedience of faith” (CCC 143). The sense of the faithful also has a role (CCC 91–93).
Dissent and development: doctrine can develop in understanding but not contradict (CCC 94).
talk: How do you respond to non-infallible teaching?
quiz: The Magisterium’s relation to the Word of God is that it…|Replaces it|Competes with it|Serves it, teaching only what has been handed on (CCC 86)|Stands above it|2|CCC 86.
Which teaching calls for “the assent of faith”?|Opinions|Local policies|Prudential advice|A dogma defined as divinely revealed (CCC 88–89)|3|CCC 88–89, 891.
Infallibility applies to…|Definitive teaching on faith and morals by the Pope or the bishops with him (CCC 891)|Any statement|Weather|Politics|0|CCC 891.
lessons.life: Read the Catechism’s sections on Magisterium (85–95).
lessons.saint: John Henry Newman: an Anglican priest who became Catholic and wrote on the development of doctrine.
lessons.mem: “He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me.” (Luke 10:16)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who decides what a rule in a game means when players disagree?” A referee. The Church has one for the faith, serving the rule, not making it.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe infallibility and give an example at each level of assent.

units.title: Scripture: the word of God
units.eq: How do we read the Bible well?

lessons.title: Inspiration and truth
lessons.idea: God is the author of Scripture and the human authors are true authors. Inspiration means the Holy Spirit moved them to write what he wished. The Bible teaches without error the truth God wanted for the sake of our salvation.
lessons.question: What does “without error” cover?
lessons.activity: “Two creation accounts” (30 min). Compare Genesis 1:1–2:4 and 2:4–25. Students list differences in order and style and the common teaching (God is Creator; humanity is made in his image; creation is good; marriage). Ask what each form of truth the author intends.
teach: Inspiration: the Holy Spirit is the author of Scripture, with human authors acting as true authors (CCC 105–107). 2 Timothy 3:16: “All Scripture is inspired by God.”
Inerrancy: the books teach “firmly, faithfully and without error that truth which God, for the sake of our salvation, wished to see confided to the Sacred Scriptures” (CCC 107; Dei Verbum 11).
This does not mean the Bible is a science textbook, nor that every statement in any sense is to be taken literally. We must ask what the author intended (CCC 109–110).
The Church also teaches that all of Scripture is a unity because of one divine author (CCC 112).
talk: What is the purpose of Scripture?
quiz: Inerrancy means…|The Bible is a dictation|Every sentence is a science fact|The Scriptures teach without error the truth God wished to put there for our salvation (CCC 107)|There is no human author|2|CCC 107.
God and human authors of Scripture relate as…|God is author and humans are true authors who used their own faculties (CCC 106)|God dictated and humans copied|Angels|Humans only|0|CCC 105–106.
To understand a biblical text we must ask…|Only the dates|What we feel|Nothing|What the author intended, considering literary form and time (CCC 109–110)|3|CCC 109–110.
lessons.life: Read Genesis 1 and Psalm 104 side by side.
lessons.saint: Jerome: who translated the Bible into Latin and wrote, “Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.”
misc: “Inerrancy means the Bible answers every scientific question.”
lessons.mem: “All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness.” (2 Timothy 3:16)
lessons.hook: Present two maps of the same city: a street map and a subway map. “Both are true; they serve different purposes.” Scripture teaches the truth God wanted for salvation.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain inspiration and inerrancy with the creation accounts as example.

lessons.title: Interpreting Scripture
lessons.idea: The Church gives three criteria for interpreting Scripture: attend to the content and unity of the whole Bible, read it within the living Tradition of the Church, and keep in mind the analogy of faith. Alongside the literal sense there are three spiritual senses.
lessons.question: What are the three criteria?
lessons.activity: “Practice on Exodus 14” (35 min). Students apply the criteria to the crossing of the Red Sea: literary form and context (history, liturgical retelling), unity (Isaiah 43, 1 Corinthians 10:1–2), Tradition (Easter Vigil, Baptism), analogy of faith (God saves). Then identify the spiritual senses (allegorical, moral, anagogical).
teach: CCC 112–114 sets three criteria: content and unity, living Tradition, analogy of faith. Complementary: literary genre, the author’s intention, historical context (CCC 109–110).
The literal sense is the foundation (CCC 116). The spiritual senses are: allegorical (how events signify Christ), moral (how to act), anagogical (our heavenly destiny) (CCC 115–117).
A medieval couplet summarizes: “The letter teaches what happened, allegory what you should believe, the moral what you should do, anagogy where you are heading.”
Exegetes are to work “so that, as it were by previous study, the judgment of the Church may mature” (CCC 119).
quiz: Which is one of the three criteria for interpreting Scripture (CCC 112–114)?|Individual intuition|Attend to the unity of the whole Scripture|The majority|The newest scholarship only|3|CCC 112.
The “anagogical” sense of Scripture points to…|Allegory|Our eternal destiny|Moral conduct|The literal event|1|CCC 117.
The literal sense is…|Allegory|Unimportant|The meaning the words convey, on which the spiritual senses build (CCC 116)|The only sense|2|CCC 116.
lessons.life: Practice the four senses on one verse.
lessons.saint: Jerome: who translated the Bible into Latin and wrote, “Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.”
misc: “A spiritual reading means ignoring the plain meaning.”
“The Church forbids reading the Bible critically.”
lessons.mem: “Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.” (Luke 24:45)
lessons.hook: Show a passage out of context (a movie quote edited). Ask: “What happens when we remove context?” Scripture needs context too.
lessons.assess: Ask students to apply the three criteria to a short passage.

lessons.title: The canon and its formation
lessons.idea: The canon is the list of inspired books. The Church, guided by the Spirit, recognized 46 Old Testament and 27 New Testament books by the late fourth century (Hippo 393, Carthage 397; confirmed by Popes). Protestants removed seven Old Testament books (the deuterocanon).
lessons.question: Who decided and why?
lessons.activity: “Canon research” (35 min). Students use a timeline of canon formation (Muratorian Fragment c. 170, Athanasius’ Easter letter 367, Hippo 393, Carthage 397, Innocent I 405, Florence 1442, Trent 1546). In pairs, they prepare an answer to a Protestant objection: “The Apocrypha was not in the Hebrew canon.” Use evidence: the Septuagint, New Testament quotations, Christian use.
teach: The Church discerned the canon through her Tradition and the Spirit’s guidance (CCC 120). The 73 books include seven deuterocanonical books (Tobit, Judith, 1–2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch) and additions to Esther and Daniel.
The earliest Christians used the Greek Septuagint, which included these books. Luther moved them to an appendix in 1534. The Jewish canon was fixed later (c. 90–100 AD), after Christianity separated.
Peter notes Paul’s letters as “Scripture” (2 Peter 3:15–16). The New Testament canon was stable by the fourth century based on apostolic origin, orthodoxy and universal use.
The Church honors Jewish tradition. Discuss respectfully.
quiz: The deuterocanonical books are…|Added at Trent without precedent|Seven Old Testament books in the Greek Septuagint that Catholics keep (CCC 120)|Apocrypha rejected by Catholics|New Testament letters|1|Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1–2 Maccabees.
Which council in 393 listed the canon?|Ephesus|Hippo|Nicaea|Trent|1|Hippo 393, Carthage 397.

A reply to “the Catholic Church added books” is that…|They were part of the Greek Bible used by early Christians, and Luther moved them in 1534|It did|They are unimportant|They were invented|0|Septuagint usage.
lessons.life: Read a short passage from Wisdom or Sirach.
lessons.saint: Augustine: who searched for truth for years before writing, “Our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
misc: “The Catholic Church added books to the Bible.”
lessons.mem: “Our beloved brother Paul wrote to you according to the wisdom given him… in all his letters.” (2 Peter 3:15–16)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who decided which books belong in the Bible?” Take guesses. “It was not decided in a single stroke or by one person.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to give three facts that support the Catholic canon.

units.title: The Old Testament and Christ
units.eq: How is Christ in the Old Testament?

lessons.title: Unity of the two Testaments
lessons.idea: The two Testaments form one story. The Old prepares for Christ and is fulfilled in him; the New is hidden in the Old. Typology — persons and events that foreshadow Christ — is the key to reading them together.
lessons.question: How is the New hidden in the Old?
lessons.activity: “Typology table” (30 min). Fill a table: type (Adam, Noah’s ark, Isaac, Passover lamb, manna, bronze serpent, Jonah, Temple), New Testament reference and fulfillment. Add one sentence on what the type teaches about Christ. Read Luke 24:44–47.
teach: “The Old Testament is a preparation for the New” (CCC 128). “The New Testament is hidden in the Old and the Old is unveiled in the New” (St Augustine; CCC 129).
Typology is the Church’s ancient method: Adam is a type of Christ (Romans 5:14), Noah’s flood of Baptism (1 Peter 3:20–21), the manna of the Eucharist (John 6:32).
The Old Testament keeps its own value (CCC 121–123). Marcion’s rejection was condemned. The Church honors the Jewish people’s covenant, which God has not revoked (CCC 839–840; Romans 11:29).
Warn against supersessionism: the Church does not teach that Jews have been replaced.
talk: How are the two Testaments one?
quiz: “The New is hidden in the Old and the Old is unveiled in the New” is from…|Pius X|Augustine|Luther|Aquinas|1|CCC 129.
A type is…|A mistake|A symbol of nothing|A prophecy only|An Old Testament person, event or thing that foreshadows Christ|3|CCC 128–130.
Which pairing is a type and fulfillment?|Moses and Nero|Adam and Christ (Romans 5:14)|David and Pilate|Noah and Herod|1|Romans 5:14.
lessons.life: Make a type–antitype chart with five rows.
lessons.saint: Irenaeus: bishop of Lyons, who defended the apostolic faith against false teachers.
misc: “The Old Testament God is angry and the New Testament God is loving.”
lessons.mem: “Everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms must be fulfilled.” (Luke 24:44)
lessons.hook: Show the first half of a mystery novel, then the last page. “The ending makes the beginning make sense.” Jesus is the ending that makes sense of the whole story.
lessons.assess: Ask students to give three types and their fulfillments.

lessons.title: Covenant history
lessons.idea: God forms a people through successive covenants: with Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David and finally the new covenant in Christ. Each covenant expands the family of God, and Jeremiah promised a new one written on hearts.
lessons.question: What is new in the new covenant?
lessons.activity: “Covenant chart” (35 min). Plot the covenants with: partner (family, tribe, nation, kingdom, all), sign (Sabbath, rainbow, circumcision, Law/Sabbath, throne, Eucharist), promise and Scripture. Read Jeremiah 31:31–34 and Luke 22:20 and note the fulfillment.
teach: Covenant with Adam (creation, Hosea 6:7), Noah (Genesis 9), Abraham (Genesis 12; 15; 17), Moses (Exodus 19–24), David (2 Samuel 7), the new covenant (Jeremiah 31; Luke 22:20) (CCC 56–64).
Each covenant widens the circle: a married pair, a household, a tribe, a nation, a kingdom, all peoples (Scott Hahn’s “family” model). Each includes oath, sign and blessings and curses.
The new covenant is “everlasting” (CCC 66). The Eucharist is its sacramental sign (CCC 1365).
Link to the unity of salvation history.
talk: What is new in the new covenant?
quiz: The new covenant is promised in…|Jeremiah 31:31–34|Psalm 1|Genesis 1|Daniel 7|0|Fulfilled in Luke 22:20.
Which covenant sign matches Noah?|Circumcision|Tablets|Throne|Rainbow|3|Genesis 9:12–17.
Covenants in Scripture differ from contracts because they…|Create family bonds with oaths|Are private|Have no signs|Are only legal|0|CCC 56–64.
lessons.life: Read Hebrews 8–9.
lessons.saint: Paul: once a persecutor, he met Christ on the road to Damascus and became the apostle to the Gentiles.
lessons.mem: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” (Jeremiah 31:33)
lessons.hook: Say: “A covenant is a family bond. Each time God widens it.” Draw circles that grow: family, tribe, nation, world.
lessons.assess: Ask students to chart three covenants with partner, sign and promise.

lessons.title: Prophecy and fulfillment
lessons.idea: The prophets announced the Messiah: born of a virgin in Bethlehem, a king from David’s line, a suffering servant, entering Jerusalem humbly. Jesus fulfills these promises, and the Gospels show it.
lessons.question: How was Jesus the fulfillment?
lessons.activity: “Study five prophecies” (35 min). Pairs examine Isaiah 7:14 / Matthew 1:22–23, Micah 5:2 / Matthew 2:5–6, Isaiah 53 / 1 Peter 2:24, Psalm 22 / Matthew 27, Zechariah 9:9 / Matthew 21:4–5. For each: context in the original, what the New Testament sees, and a caution (not every connection is literal).
teach: Messianic prophecy is part of the preparation for Christ (CCC 522–524, 702–716). Messiah (Hebrew) and Christ (Greek) mean “anointed one.”
The Gospels use many Old Testament texts to show Jesus’ identity. Some are direct predictions (Micah 5:2), others typological or deeper meanings (Hosea 11:1 / Matthew 2:15).
Isaiah 53 is read by the Church as the Servant who suffers for sins (CCC 601). Psalm 22 begins with the cry Jesus uttered on the Cross.
Be fair to Jewish readings of these passages and to critical questions about translation (e.g., almah in Isaiah 7:14 translated parthenos in the Septuagint).
talk: How do you respond to “vague” objections?
quiz: Micah 5:2 foretells…|The birthplace of the Messiah, Bethlehem|The Ascension|The flight into Egypt|The Passion|0|Matthew 2:5–6.

A caution about messianic proofs is that…|There are none|Some fulfillments are typological or deeper meanings rather than literal predictions|They are unimportant|All are literal|1|e.g., Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15.
Isaiah 53 is read by the Church as…|The Servant who suffers for sins (CCC 601)|A war song|A description of Cyrus|A genealogy|0|CCC 601.
lessons.life: Choose five prophecies and trace the New Testament fulfilments.
lessons.saint: John the Baptist: the forerunner who prepared the way and pointed to Christ.
lessons.mem: “But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel.” (Micah 5:2)
lessons.hook: Say: “Imagine if someone predicted details of your life 700 years before you were born.” Introduce Micah 5:2.
lessons.assess: Ask students to present two prophecies with their fulfillments and one caution.

units.title: Who is Jesus Christ?
units.eq: Who do you say that I am?

lessons.title: The historical Jesus
lessons.idea: The Gospels are reliable historical witnesses to the Jesus who lived. Beyond the Gospels, ancient writers such as Tacitus, Josephus and Pliny mention him. The evangelists wrote within decades of the events, using eyewitness testimony.
lessons.question: What do non-Christian sources say?
lessons.activity: “External testimony” (30 min). Students read short excerpts from Tacitus (Annals 15.44), Josephus (Antiquities 18.3 and 20.9), Pliny the Younger (Letter 10.96), and compare them to Gospel details. Make a list of what independent writers confirm (crucified under Pilate, followers called Christians, worshiped as God).
teach: The Church holds that the Gospels “faithfully hand on what Jesus … did and taught for the eternal salvation of men” (CCC 126; Dei Verbum 19). They are history shaped by faith.

Manuscript evidence: thousands of early copies, the earliest fragments within decades (P52, c. 125 AD). The Gospels were written within about 30–70 years of the events, while eyewitnesses lived (Luke 1:1–4).
Non-Christian sources: Tacitus, Josephus (parts debated), Pliny, Suetonius. Few scholars today doubt that Jesus existed and was crucified under Pilate.
Faith is not just history; but faith is not against history.
talk: What is the criterion of embarrassment?
quiz: Which source outside Christianity mentions Jesus’ execution under Pilate?|Plato|Virgil|Tacitus (Annals 15.44)|Homer|2|Tacitus c. 116.
The earliest New Testament manuscript fragments date from…|The second century (e.g., P52)|The Middle Ages|The Reformation|The tenth century|0|P52 c. 125.
Luke 1:1–4 shows the Gospel’s method as…|Dream|Rumor|Myth|Careful investigation of eyewitness testimony|3|Luke 1:1–4.
lessons.life: Read Tacitus and Josephus excerpts.
lessons.saint: Luke: the physician and evangelist who carefully investigated the story of Jesus.
misc: “There’s no evidence outside the Bible that Jesus existed.”
lessons.mem: “It seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you.” (Luke 1:3)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How do historians know about Julius Caesar?” By documents, manuscripts and other sources. Apply the same tools to Jesus.
lessons.assess: Ask students to present three pieces of evidence for the historical Jesus.

lessons.title: True God and true man
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, one divine Person with two natures, human and divine, without confusion or division. Councils from Nicaea to Chalcedon defended this against heresies.
lessons.question: Why does it matter that Jesus is both?
lessons.activity: “Councils and heresies” (35 min). Match each heresy to the council and the truth defended: Arianism (Nicaea 325), Apollinarianism (Constantinople 381), Nestorianism (Ephesus 431), Monophysitism (Chalcedon 451), Monothelitism (Constantinople III 681). Write a one-sentence summary of Chalcedon’s formula.
teach: Chalcedon (451): “one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, only-begotten, in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation” (CCC 467).
Jesus has a human body, soul, intellect and will (CCC 470–483). He is not a human person with a divine mask but the divine Person who assumed human nature.
The Philippians hymn (2:5–11) describes the self-emptying of the Son. “Emptying” is not losing divinity but taking the form of a servant.
Take care to connect doctrine to devotion: because God became man, our humanity is redeemed (CCC 460).
quiz: Chalcedon taught that Christ is…|One nature|Two persons|One divine Person in two natures, divine and human|A creature|2|CCC 467.
Docetism taught that Christ…|Was truly human|Only seemed to have a body|Was a man|Was divine|1|CCC 465.
Why does it matter that Christ is truly human?|He needed to learn|It is poetic|Because only a true man could save mankind from within (CCC 470–478)|It does not|2|CCC 470–478.
lessons.life: Read the Chalcedonian definition.
lessons.saint: Leo the Great: the pope whose letter on Christ’s two natures guided the Council of Chalcedon.
misc: “Jesus only became God after the resurrection.”
lessons.mem: “Though he was in the form of God, [he] did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself.” (Philippians 2:6–7)
lessons.hook: Read Philippians 2:5–11. Ask: “What does it mean that he ‘emptied himself’ and still remained God?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Chalcedon’s formula and one heresy it rejected.

lessons.title: Jesus’ self-understanding
lessons.idea: Jesus’ words and deeds show who he understood himself to be: he forgave sins, claimed to be Lord of the Sabbath, called God his Father, and said “I AM.” Either he was what he claimed or something else; the Church believes he is the Son of God.
lessons.question: What did Jesus claim?
lessons.activity: “I AM sayings” (30 min). Collect Jesus’ seven “I AM” sayings in John (bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way/truth/life, vine) and “Before Abraham was, I am” (8:58). Students note which Old Testament images each echoes and which title (Messiah, Son of God, Son of Man, Lord) fits.
teach: Titles: Christ (Messiah), Son of God, Son of Man, Lord (CCC 436–455). “Son of Man” (Daniel 7:13–14) is Jesus’ own preferred title, expressing both humanity and divine glory.
Jesus claims divine prerogatives: forgiving sins (Mark 2:5–7), authority over the Sabbath (Mark 2:28), “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), calling God “Abba” (Mark 14:36).
C. S. Lewis’ “trilemma” (liar, lunatic, Lord) is a popular argument but should be used carefully, since it omits “legend.” Consider the evidence on the Gospels’ reliability.
Faith in Christ’s divinity is a gift as well as a conclusion.
talk: What does it mean to follow?
quiz: In Mark 2, forgiving sins was a claim of divine authority because…|Only God can forgive sins (Mark 2:7)|It was routine|It was symbolic|Priests do it|0|Mark 2:5–10.
“Son of Man” in Jesus’ usage evokes…|A rabbi|Daniel 7’s figure given dominion by God, a title of glory|A mere human|A simple phrase|1|Daniel 7:13–14.
Which “I AM” saying echoes the divine name?|“Blessed are the poor”|“Follow me”|“Come and see”|“Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58)|3|John 8:58.
lessons.life: List Jesus’s “I AM” sayings in John.
lessons.saint: Thomas: the apostle who doubted, then confessed, “My Lord and my God.”
lessons.mem: “I and the Father are one.” (John 10:30)
lessons.hook: Read Mark 2:1–12. Ask: “What is the objection of the scribes? Is it reasonable?” Only God can forgive sins.
lessons.assess: Ask students to list three ways Jesus claimed divine authority and explain their significance.

units.title: The mission of Jesus
units.eq: What did he come to do?

lessons.title: Teacher of the kingdom
lessons.idea: Jesus began his ministry proclaiming, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.” His teaching in parables and the Sermon on the Mount reveals the Kingdom and calls for conversion.
lessons.question: What is the kingdom?
lessons.activity: “Analyze three parables” (35 min). Groups study the sower (Mark 4), the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21–35) and the great banquet (Luke 14:15–24). For each: setting, surprise, what it says about the Kingdom, and a challenge. Create a one-minute dramatization.
teach: The Kingdom of God is the central message (CCC 541–546). It is a gift, grows like a seed, and requires conversion (Mark 1:15). It is already present in Jesus and will come in fullness at the end (CCC 2816).
Parables use everyday images to call hearers to decide (CCC 546). Jesus invites all, “especially the poor and sinners” (CCC 543).
The Sermon on the Mount sets out the Kingdom’s ethic (Matthew 5–7).
The Church is the seed and beginning of the Kingdom on earth (CCC 541, 768).
quiz: The Kingdom of God in Jesus’ preaching is…|God’s reign, present in Christ and still to come in fullness (CCC 541–546)|A philosophy|Only heaven|A political state|0|CCC 541–546.
Parables use ordinary images to…|Entertain|Hide the Gospel|Teach farming|Reveal and challenge, calling hearers to decide (CCC 546)|3|CCC 546.
The Sermon on the Mount is…|A miracle|A parable|A genealogy|The charter of the New Law (CCC 1966)|3|Matthew 5–7.
lessons.life: Interpret three parables with the Catechism.
lessons.saint: Francis: who gave up wealth to follow Christ in poverty and joy and loved creation.
misc: “The Kingdom of God is only in heaven.”
lessons.mem: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.” (Mark 1:15)
lessons.hook: Read Mark 1:14–15. Ask: “What would it mean if a king’s rule were arriving in your town?” Prepare your life.
lessons.assess: Ask students to retell a parable and say what it teaches about the Kingdom.

lessons.title: Signs and miracles
lessons.idea: Jesus’ miracles are signs that the Kingdom has come. They show his power over nature, sin, sickness and death, and invite faith. Skeptics such as Hume argue against miracles; Christians respond that if God exists, miracles are possible and testimony can establish them.
lessons.question: Are miracles credible?
lessons.activity: “Respond to a skeptic” (35 min). Students respond to Hume’s argument (“a miracle is a violation of laws of nature, and testimony is never enough”). In pairs, they draft a short reply: laws describe regular causes, not what God can do; testimony can be strong; probability must consider the evidence. Debate.
teach: Miracles accompany Jesus’ word and show the Kingdom has begun (CCC 547–550). They are “signs” of his identity, not tricks (CCC 548).
Faith is the response; Jesus often asks for it before a healing (Mark 5:34). Miracles do not force belief (John 12:37).
Philosophically, if God exists he can act in the world (CCC 156). Hume’s argument has been criticized as circular. Lourdes and Church-investigated healings continue (CCC 2003).
The greatest miracle is the Resurrection (CCC 647).
quiz: A “sign” in John’s Gospel is…|A work that points beyond itself to who Jesus is (John 2:11)|A prophecy|A magic trick|A hallucination|0|John 2:11.

Hume’s argument against miracles has been criticized because it…|Is certainly right|Is scientific|Uses Scripture|Assumes in advance that miracles do not occur, so no testimony could be enough|3|Common critique.
Which best describes the purpose of Jesus’ miracles?|To manifest the Kingdom and invite faith (CCC 547–550)|To cause fear|To show off|To pay debts|0|CCC 547–550.
lessons.life: Read a modern, approved miracle account (Lourdes).
lessons.saint: Bernadette: a poor girl who saw Mary at Lourdes and prayed the Rosary.
lessons.mem: “This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him.” (John 2:11)
lessons.hook: Read John 2:11 (“the first of his signs”). Ask: “A sign points to something. What does the wedding wine point to?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what a sign is and answer one objection.

lessons.title: Why did Jesus come?
lessons.idea: Why did the Son of God become man? To save us by reconciling us to God, to show us God’s love, to be our model of holiness and to make us “partakers of the divine nature.” The Church Fathers: “God became man so that man might become God.”
lessons.question: What does he save us from?
lessons.activity: “Four reasons” statement (25 min). Students write a statement answering “Why did Jesus come?” in four parts, with a verse for each (John 3:16; 1 John 4:9–10; John 13:15; 2 Peter 1:4). Share and compare.
teach: CCC 456–460 gives four reasons: to save us by reconciling us with God, to show us God’s love, to be our model of holiness, and to make us “partakers of the divine nature.”
Athanasius: “The Son of God became man so that we might become God” (CCC 460) — meaning sharing in God’s life by grace, not becoming God by nature.
The Incarnation is the center of the whole plan of redemption. The New Testament uses many images: ransom, reconciliation, adoption.
Link to the Christmas season and to Easter: one mystery.
quiz: Which is NOT one of the four reasons the Word became flesh (CCC 457–460)?|To abolish the Old Testament|To show us God’s love|To be our model of holiness|To save us by reconciling us with God|0|CCC 457–460.
Athanasius’ line “God became man that man might become god” means…|Humans are divine|We become God by nature|We share by grace in God’s life (CCC 460)|Nothing|2|CCC 460.
John 3:16 stresses that the Incarnation arises from…|Human merit|Necessity|Fate|God’s love|3|John 3:16.
lessons.life: Write your own summary of why Jesus came.
lessons.saint: Athanasius: bishop of Alexandria, who defended the divinity of Christ through repeated exiles.
misc: “Jesus came only to teach a moral code.”
lessons.mem: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.” (John 3:16)
lessons.hook: Read John 3:16. Ask: “What would you do for someone you love? What did God do?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to give the four reasons for the Incarnation with a verse each.

units.title: The Paschal Mystery
units.eq: What happened on Calvary and Easter?

lessons.title: Why did Jesus die?
lessons.idea: Jesus died for our sins, in accordance with the Scriptures, as a sacrifice freely offered out of love. The New Testament and the Church use several images — ransom, sacrifice, satisfaction, expiation — none of which exhausts the mystery.
lessons.question: What does “atonement” mean?
lessons.activity: “Compare theories of atonement” (35 min). Students compare: ransom (Origen), satisfaction (Anselm), penal substitution, moral influence (Abelard), Christus Victor. For each: the idea, a verse, a strength and a weakness. The Church has not defined one theory; the Catechism uses several (CCC 615–618).
teach: Christ died “for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3; CCC 599–605). His death fulfills Isaiah 53 and was freely accepted (CCC 609–614).

The Church does not teach that the Father is a cruel judge who punishes an innocent victim. The Father gives his Son; the Son freely offers himself; it is one act of love of the Trinity (CCC 603–605).
Images: redemption (a price paid), sacrifice, expiation, reconciliation (CCC 615–618). The Cross makes possible our salvation and is renewed in the Mass.
Handle “penal substitution” carefully; Catholic teaching emphasizes love and satisfaction rather than a punishment transferred.
talk: What does it demand of us?
quiz: Which model of the Cross appears in Mark 10:45?|Exchange|Magic|Moral example only|Ransom|3|Mark 10:45.

The Catholic Church does not teach that…|Christ’s death is a sacrifice of love|The Father is cruel and demands a victim; the Father and Son act in one love (CCC 603–605)|Christ freely gave himself|Sin has consequences|1|CCC 603–605.
Christus Victor emphasizes…|Christ’s victory over sin and death|Nothing|Moral influence only|Satisfaction only|0|One image among several.
lessons.life: Contemplate the Cross for 10 minutes.
lessons.saint: Paul of the Cross: a priest who preached the Passion of Christ and founded the Passionists.
misc: “Jesus’ death was only a moral example.”
lessons.mem: “For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45)
lessons.hook: Show an object and ask: “What is the cost of love?” A parent’s sacrifice. Look at Mark 10:45: “to give his life as a ransom for many.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe two models of atonement and avoid a common distortion.

lessons.title: The Resurrection
lessons.idea: Jesus rose bodily on the third day. It is both a historical event and a transcendent mystery. The evidence — the empty tomb, the appearances to many people, and the transformation of the disciples — led to the Church’s faith.
lessons.question: How strong is the evidence?
lessons.activity: “Weigh the evidence” debate (40 min). Teams argue for and against the proposition “The best explanation of the evidence is that Jesus rose from the dead.” Teams use 1 Corinthians 15:3–8, Luke 24, the empty tomb, the appearances, the disciples’ transformation, and alternatives (hallucination, theft, swoon, myth). Conclude with the Church’s claim.
teach: The Resurrection is a historical event attested by signs and also transcends history (CCC 639–647). Paul lists witnesses, including more than 500 at once, most still alive (1 Corinthians 15:3–8).
Alternatives struggle: hallucinations don’t explain group appearances or the empty tomb; theft doesn’t explain the transformation; swoon theory fails given Roman execution.
The first witnesses were women, an unlikely invention in that culture. The disciples were willing to die for it.
The Resurrection invites faith; it is not coercive proof (CCC 644). It is the foundation of Christian hope (CCC 651–655).
talk: What does it mean for us?
quiz: Which line of evidence is strongest for the first witnesses being sincere?|They hid|They gained wealth|They died for what they proclaimed|They were soldiers|2|Martyrdom of apostles.

The first witnesses being women is significant because…|It was typical|In that culture women’s testimony counted little, so it is unlikely to be invented|They were not present|It does not matter|1|Matthew 28; John 20.
The Resurrection is both…|Historical and transcendent (CCC 639–647)|Only legend|Only spiritual|Only symbolic|0|CCC 639–647.
lessons.life: Read 1 Corinthians 15 aloud.
lessons.saint: Paul: once a persecutor, he met Christ on the road to Damascus and became the apostle to the Gentiles.
misc: “The Resurrection was only a spiritual experience.”
lessons.mem: “If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.” (1 Corinthians 15:14)
lessons.hook: Say: “If you wanted to prove a big claim in court, you would want witnesses, physical evidence, and motive.” Apply to the Resurrection.
lessons.assess: Ask students to present evidence for the Resurrection and respond to one alternative.

lessons.title: Ascension and Parousia
lessons.idea: Jesus ascended to the Father and sits at his right hand; he will return in glory at the Parousia to judge the living and the dead. Until then, he is present in his Church and the sacraments, and we live in hopeful expectation.
lessons.question: What does it mean?
lessons.activity: “Creed commentary” (30 min). Students write a short commentary on the lines “He ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father; he will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead.” Define each phrase and say how it affects daily life.
teach: The Ascension is Christ’s enthronement in glory and our hope to follow (CCC 659–667). “The right hand of the Father” means authority and honor.
The Parousia, the second coming, will bring final judgment and the fullness of the Kingdom (CCC 668–679). No one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36).
In the meantime, the Church lives between Christ’s first and second comings (CCC 671–672).
Resist speculation about dates, as Jesus warns.
quiz: The Ascension is…|His enthronement in glory, from which he remains with the Church (CCC 659–667)|A funeral|The end of Christ’s presence|A myth|0|CCC 659–667.
The Parousia is…|His birth|A feast|His baptism|The Second Coming of Christ in glory (CCC 668–679)|3|CCC 668–679.
Jesus teaches about the day of his return that…|No one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36)|It is next year|It is yesterday|It is calculable|0|Matthew 24:36.
lessons.life: Write a creed paragraph on the Ascension.
lessons.saint: Luke: the physician and evangelist who carefully investigated the story of Jesus.
misc: “We can calculate the date of the Second Coming.”
lessons.mem: “This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” (Acts 1:11)
lessons.hook: Read Acts 1:9–11. Ask: “Why did the angels ask, ‘Why do you stand looking into heaven?’” We are meant to act while we wait.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the Ascension and the Parousia and how they shape Christian life.

lessons.title: Faith and discipleship
lessons.idea: Following Jesus means denying ourselves, taking up the cross daily and following him. Discipleship is a response to a call, a relationship and a way of life. The call stories show how Jesus invites ordinary people.
lessons.question: What does it cost?
lessons.activity: “Call story reflection” (30 min). Students read three call stories (Matthew 4:18–22, Luke 5:1–11, John 1:35–51). They note what Jesus does, the response, the cost. Then write about a moment they sensed an invitation from God.
teach: Christian life is following Christ (CCC 520, 1694). “If any man would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me” (Luke 9:23).
All are called to holiness (CCC 2013–2015). The call comes from God’s initiative and requires our free response (CCC 1812–1829).
The cross is not self-hatred but self-giving love. The Beatitudes show the path (CCC 1716–1724).
Discipleship is lived in community, the Church, with the sacraments and prayer.
quiz: Luke 9:23 calls disciples to…|Deny themselves, take up the cross daily and follow|Obey law only|Comfort|Leave society|0|Luke 9:23.
The cross in the Christian life is…|Self-hatred|Seeking pain|A symbol only|Self-giving love united to Christ (CCC 618)|3|CCC 618.
All are called to…|Only marriage|Only priesthood|Holiness (CCC 2013)|Nothing|2|CCC 2013.
lessons.life: Choose one cross to carry this week.
lessons.saint: Ignatius: a soldier turned priest whose Spiritual Exercises teach discernment.
misc: “Taking up the cross means seeking suffering.”
lessons.mem: “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.” (Luke 9:23)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 9:23. Ask: “What does ‘take up your cross daily’ look like for a teenager?” Honest answers.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what discipleship asks and give a concrete example.

lessons.title: Grace and justification
lessons.idea: We are justified by grace through faith, not by our own works. Grace is a free gift of God’s life that forgives sin, makes us holy and enables good works. We cooperate with grace, and God rewards what he himself accomplishes in us.
lessons.question: What is grace?
lessons.activity: “Clear up misunderstandings” (35 min). Students sort statements: “Catholics think they earn salvation” (false), “Faith alone with no response” (not Catholic), “Grace first, faith responds, works flow” (Catholic). Read Ephesians 2:8–10 and James 2:24 and harmonize. Write a two-sentence explanation of justification.
teach: Justification is “the most excellent work of God’s love” (CCC 1994). It is granted in Baptism and takes away sin and makes us sharers in divine life (CCC 1987–1995).

Grace is a free, undeserved gift (CCC 1996–2005). We cannot merit the first grace; afterwards we merit rewards by grace (CCC 2006–2011). “It is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

Ephesians 2:8–10: “by grace you have been saved through faith… for good works.” James 2:24 stresses that faith is alive through works. The Joint Declaration on Justification (1999) with Lutherans shows common ground.
Emphasize hope and humility: salvation is gift and response.
talk: How do faith and works relate?
quiz: Which statement is Catholic?|Faith has no effect|Justification is God’s free gift by grace, received through faith that works in love (CCC 1987–1995; Galatians 5:6)|Once saved always saved|We are saved by works alone|1|CCC 1987–1995.
Merit in Catholic teaching rests on…|Luck|Our own power|God’s grace enabling our good acts (CCC 2006–2011)|Law|2|CCC 2006–2011.
The 1999 Joint Declaration on Justification was between…|Catholics and Lutherans|Anglicans and Methodists|Catholics and Orthodox|Jews and Christians|0|1999.
lessons.life: Pray the Act of Contrition with attention to grace.
lessons.saint: Augustine: who searched for truth for years before writing, “Our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
lessons.mem: “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” (Ephesians 2:8)
lessons.hook: Say: “A gift cannot be earned. But you can open it or leave it on the table.” Grace is like that.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the Catholic view of grace, faith and works.

lessons.title: Prayer with the Gospels
lessons.idea: We can pray with the Gospels by entering the scene, meeting Jesus and speaking with him. Lectio divina (read, meditate, pray, contemplate) and Ignatian contemplation (imagining the scene with the senses) are two ancient methods.
lessons.question: How do we encounter Christ?
lessons.activity: “Lectio divina” (35 min). Guide the class through lectio on Luke 24:13–35 in four movements: read and notice a word; meditate; pray a response; rest. Then try an Ignatian imagination exercise: place yourself in the scene as a disciple. Journal.
teach: Lectio divina: lectio (read), meditatio (meditate), oratio (pray), contemplatio (rest) (CCC 2705–2708). The practice is rooted in the Fathers and monasteries.
Ignatian contemplation uses imagination: see, hear, touch the scene and speak with Jesus (CCC 2708, 2715). Jesus is the one who “looks at us”.
The Jesus Prayer anchors attention (CCC 2616). Gospel prayer should lead to action.
Suggest students pray with the Sunday Gospel during the week.
quiz: Lectio divina has movements of…|Ask, seek, knock|Tell, listen, vote|Sing, dance, fast|Read, meditate, pray, contemplate|3|CCC 2705–2708.
Ignatian contemplation uses…|Statistics|Imagination to enter a Gospel scene and speak with Christ|Silence only|Memorization|1|Spiritual Exercises.
The Emmaus story shows Jesus…|Teaching nothing|Explaining Scripture and being known in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:13–35)|Leaving|Hiding|1|Luke 24.
lessons.life: Do lectio divina every day this week with one Gospel scene.
lessons.saint: Ignatius: a soldier turned priest whose Spiritual Exercises teach discernment.
misc: “Imagination in prayer is making things up.”
lessons.mem: “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road?” (Luke 24:32)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 24:13–35 slowly. Ask: “If you were walking beside Jesus on the road to Emmaus, what would you say?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to practice a brief lectio and explain the four movements.

units.title: Hard questions about the Church
units.eq: Why does the Church teach what it teaches?

lessons.title: Sinners in the Church: the abuse crisis and reform
lessons.idea: The Church is holy and made of sinners. When leaders harm the vulnerable or hide it, that is a grave sin that must be faced with truth, justice and care for victims.
lessons.question: How can the Church be holy when some leaders did terrible things?
lessons.activity: List what a safe community looks like (rules, reporting, accountability, care for victims).
teach: Sensitive topic: follow your school’s safe-environment policy and let students step out. Never ask anyone to share personal experiences.

Jesus said it would be better for someone to have a millstone hung around their neck than to cause a little one to stumble (Luke 17:2; Matthew 18:6). Abuse of a minor is a grave sin and a crime. Hiding it makes it worse.

The Church is holy through Christ, but its members, including clergy, are sinners (CCC 823, 827). In the United States the bishops adopted a Charter for the Protection of Children and Young People in 2002 and require safe-environment training and background checks. Reports and reforms continue.

The right response is truth, justice, reporting to civil authorities, care for survivors, and reform. It is not leaving every vulnerable person without the Church’s care, nor pretending nothing happened.
talk: What makes a community safe for children?
Why does covering up a wrong often hurt people more than the original wrong?
How can people stay close to Christ when they are angry with leaders of the Church?
quiz: What did the U.S. bishops adopt in 2002?|A new liturgy|The Charter for the Protection of Children and Young People|A new Catechism|A ban on all youth programs|1|It requires reporting and safe-environment training.
Jesus’ words about those who cause “little ones” to stumble show that…|Only judges can speak of it|Harming children is gravely wrong|It is minor|It should be kept private|1|Luke 17:2.
The Church is “holy” because…|It has never failed|Every member is perfect|Its leaders are sinless|Christ makes it holy, even with sinful members|3|CCC 823.
lessons.life: Learn who to tell if you or a friend is being hurt, and pray for survivors of abuse.
lessons.saint: Josephine Bakhita: a survivor of slavery and violence who became a sister, patron of survivors of trafficking.
misc: “The Church has never dealt with the problem.”
“A few bad priests means everything the Church teaches is false.”
lessons.mem: “Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me.” (Matthew 18:5)
lessons.hook: Say plainly that this lesson is about real harm and real accountability, and that anyone may step out. Follow your diocese’s safe-environment policy.
lessons.assess: Ask students to list what a safe community requires and where to report concerns.

lessons.title: Why can’t women be priests?
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that only baptized men are ordained priests, following Christ’s choice of the Twelve, and that this does not mean women are less valuable. Women have always been central to the Church.
lessons.question: Is this fair?
lessons.activity: List the roles of women in the Church, from Mary to the Doctors of the Church.
teach: The Catechism teaches that “only a baptized man validly receives sacred ordination” (CCC 1577), because Christ chose men as apostles and the Church has no authority to change it (Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, St John Paul II, 1994).
The Church does not say women are less than men. Equal in dignity (CCC 2334), the sexes have different callings. Mary, the greatest of all the saints, was not a priest.

Women have led the Church as saints, Doctors of the Church (Catherine of Siena, Teresa of Avila, Thérèse of Lisieux, Hildegard of Bingen), abbesses, theologians, missionaries and heads of hospitals and schools.
Many sincerely disagree. Understand the teaching, then discuss respectfully. Some Christian communities have different practices, but the Catholic and Orthodox Churches do not ordain women priests.
talk: What does it mean that people can be equal in dignity and different in roles?
Which woman in the Church’s history do you admire most, and why?
How should we speak with someone who thinks the teaching is unjust?
quiz: Which document restated that the Church cannot ordain women?|Ordinatio Sacerdotalis (1994)|Humanae Vitae|Lumen Fidei|Rerum Novarum|0|St John Paul II.
Who among these is a woman Doctor of the Church?|Monica|Teresa of Avila|Clare of Assisi|Rita|1|Doctors include Teresa of Avila, Catherine of Siena and Thérèse.
The Catechism says the sexes are…|Equal in dignity and different|Identical in every role|Unequal in dignity|Unrelated|0|CCC 2334.
lessons.life: Learn the story of one woman Doctor of the Church and share it.
lessons.saint: Catherine of Siena: a lay Dominican who advised popes and was named Doctor of the Church.
misc: “Women have no real role in the Church.”
lessons.mem: “Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord.” (Luke 1:38)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Name women who shaped the Church.” List them before addressing the question of ordination.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the Church’s reasons for ordaining only men and name three roles women hold.

lessons.title: Celibacy: why don’t Catholic priests marry?
lessons.idea: Priestly celibacy is a discipline, not a doctrine, and a gift of undivided love for Christ and the Church. In the Eastern Catholic Churches, married men can be ordained.
lessons.question: Why does the Latin Church ask this of priests?
lessons.activity: Compare the reasons for a celibate priesthood with the reasons for a married one.
teach: Celibacy is a discipline of the Latin Church, not a dogma (CCC 1579–1580). Eastern Catholic priests may be married, though bishops are celibate, and some married former Anglican or Episcopal clergy have been ordained Catholic priests.
Jesus and St Paul both lived and praised chosen celibacy for the Kingdom (Matthew 19:12; 1 Corinthians 7). The Church sees it as total, undivided giving (CCC 1579).

It has costs: loneliness, struggles and failures. The Church asks that men be well formed and supported. The question of whether the discipline should change is a legitimate one, but only the pope and the Church can change it.
Don’t confuse celibacy with the abuse crisis. Most abuse happens in families and many institutions; the answer is accountability and formation.
talk: What might someone gain and lose in giving up marriage for a mission?
Why would the Church treat this as a discipline rather than a doctrine?
How can we support the priests we know?
quiz: Is priestly celibacy a dogma?|It is a law of the Gospels|No, it is a discipline|Yes, an infallible doctrine|It is a sacrament|1|CCC 1579.
Which Catholics may ordain married men as priests?|Only monks|None|Eastern Catholic Churches|Only the Latin Church|2|Eastern practice.
Jesus spoke of those who “make themselves eunuchs” in…|Matthew 19:12|Acts 2:38|Luke 1:28|John 3:16|0|Chosen celibacy for the Kingdom.
lessons.life: Write a thank-you note to a priest or religious who has helped you.
lessons.saint: John Vianney: the Curé of Ars, a priest who gave everything to his parish and heard confessions up to sixteen hours a day.
misc: “Celibacy is a Church dogma that can never change.”
lessons.mem: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this receive it.” (Matthew 19:12)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you give up for something you loved completely?” Introduce celibacy as a gift with a purpose.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why celibacy is a discipline and where Eastern Catholic priests differ.

units.title: How the faith grows and is handed on
units.eq: How does the Church hand on the faith faithfully?

lessons.title: Development of doctrine
lessons.idea: The Church understands the faith more deeply over time while teaching the same truth. Doctrine develops like a seed growing into a tree, never contradicting what came before.
lessons.question: How can teaching grow without changing?
lessons.activity: Trace the development of one doctrine, like the Trinity or Mary as Mother of God, across councils. Make a timeline showing what was clarified.
teach: The deposit of faith was complete with the apostles (CCC 66, 84). Over time the Church understands it more fully with the help of the Spirit (CCC 94; Dei Verbum 8).
Growth comes through contemplation, study, lived experience and the Magisterium (CCC 94). The Council of Nicaea clarified, not invented, belief in Christ’s divinity.
Newman wrote that a true development preserves the same type and principles; a corruption does not (Essay on Development). Use his seven notes as a guide.
Distinguish doctrine (which develops) from discipline (which can change). Examples: fasting rules, vernacular Mass.
talk: Can you think of a teaching that was clarified over time?
What is the difference between a development and a change?
Why does the Church need a living teacher?
quiz: A true development of doctrine…|Ignores Scripture|Invents a new revelation|Keeps the same truth and deepens it|Reverses an earlier teaching|2|CCC 94.
Who wrote an influential Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine?|Teresa of Ávila|John Henry Newman|Francis de Sales|Thomas Aquinas|1|Newman, 1845.
Which can change?|The resurrection|The Creed|Dogma of the Trinity|Discipline|3|CCC 83.
lessons.life: Pick a doctrine and read how it was explained in a council or a Father.
lessons.saint: John Henry Newman: a convert and scholar who studied how doctrine grows.
misc: “The Church changes its teaching whenever it wants.”
“Nothing in the faith has ever been explained more deeply.”
lessons.mem: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.” (John 16:13)
lessons.hook: Show a seed and a tree. Ask: “Is the tree something new, or the seed grown up?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain development of doctrine and distinguish it from change.

lessons.title: Dogma and the hierarchy of truths
lessons.idea: Dogmas are truths the Church teaches as revealed by God. Not all truths are equally central: the heart of the faith is the Trinity, Christ and our salvation. All truths belong together.
lessons.question: What is a dogma and why do we have them?
lessons.activity: Sort statements into dogma, doctrine, discipline and opinion. Draw a pyramid with the center of the faith at the top and ordered truths below it.
teach: A dogma is a truth contained in Revelation that the Church defines (CCC 88–90). Dogmas are like lights on the path: they illuminate and secure the faith (CCC 89).
There is an order, or “hierarchy,” of truths (CCC 90; Unitatis Redintegratio 11). The mystery of the Trinity and Christ stand at the center (CCC 234, 426).
Teachings can be defined (dogma), taught definitively, taught authoritatively, or be pastoral guidance. Respond with the appropriate assent (CCC 891–892).
Heresy is the obstinate denial of a revealed truth; it harms unity and faith (CCC 2089).
talk: Why might a Church define a dogma?
What is at the center of our faith?
How can a hierarchy of truths help us in dialogue?
quiz: A dogma is…|A truth the Church defines as revealed|A rule of dress|A song|A feast|0|CCC 88.
At the center of the hierarchy of truths is…|A custom|A building|A holiday|The Trinity and Christ|3|CCC 234.
Heresy is…|A question|Obstinate denial of a revealed truth|A prayer|A doubt|1|CCC 2089.
lessons.life: Choose one dogma and write why it matters for your life.
lessons.saint: Athanasius: he held firmly to the dogma of Christ’s divinity at great personal cost.
lessons.mem: “You will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” (John 8:32)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What are the rules that cannot change in a game, and which can?” Link to dogma and discipline.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain dogma, hierarchy of truths and heresy.

lessons.title: The sense of the faithful and the work of the laity in handing on the faith
lessons.idea: All the baptized receive the Spirit and share in handing on the faith. The sense of the faithful, parents, teachers and catechists, and the witness of ordinary people help keep the faith alive.
lessons.question: How do ordinary Catholics hand on the faith?
lessons.activity: Interview a grandparent, catechist or parent about who passed on the faith to them. Write a short thank-you and a plan for passing it on.
teach: The whole body of the faithful, who have an anointing from the Holy One, cannot err in believing (CCC 91–93; 1 John 2:20). This “sense of the faith” works under the guidance of the Magisterium.
The laity share in Christ’s prophetic office by witness and teaching (CCC 904–907). Parents are the first teachers (CCC 2221–2226).
Catechists, teachers, godparents and friends hand on the faith. Women and men have done this since the first generations.
It is not majority opinion. The sense of the faith is discerned by the Church and is linked to Tradition and Scripture.
talk: Who handed the faith to you?
How can you hand on your faith to someone younger?
Why is the sense of the faith not the same as a poll?
quiz: Parents are…|The first teachers of the faith|Only helpers|Replaced by the school|Not involved|0|CCC 2223.
The sense of the faith means…|A vote|The body of the faithful believes the truth under the Spirit|A poll|A feeling|1|CCC 92.
Which is a way to hand on the faith?|Hiding|Silence only|Money|Witness and teaching|3|CCC 905.
lessons.life: Write a note of thanks to someone who passed the faith on to you, and share a prayer with someone younger.
lessons.saint: Monica: a mother whose prayers helped her son Augustine return to faith.
lessons.mem: “But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.” (1 John 2:20)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who taught you to pray?” Collect names and notice how many are ordinary people.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the sense of the faith and how they will pass on the faith.
